lesson.title: Finding the conclusion

lead.text: Take the doorstep remark again: “You should take an umbrella, because the forecast says rain.” It holds two claims, and they do different jobs. One is what the speaker wants you to accept, that you should take an umbrella. The other is offered to make that easier to accept, that the forecast says rain.

Claims put together like this make an argument. In everyday speech the word often means a quarrel, but in logic it only means reasons given for a claim. The claim the argument is trying to get you to accept is its conclusion. Each claim offered in support of it is a premise. Here the conclusion is that you should take an umbrella, and the one premise is the forecast.

The test for which is which does not depend on the order of the sentences or on how they are built. Ask what the speaker wants you to believe or to do, and the answer is the conclusion. Whatever has been put forward to help is a premise. That test is worth trying on another remark.
Here is a remark with the aim and the reason both in it. Ask what the speaker wants you to accept.
That last remark had a small word in the middle doing quiet work. People leave clues like it all the time, and learning to spot them makes the test from the last screen quicker.

Some words usually lead into a conclusion, such as “so”, “thus” and “hence”. In “The oven is cold, so dinner will be late”, the word “so” points ahead to where the speaker is going. Other words usually lead into a premise, such as “because”, “since” and “given that”. In “I'm taking the bus, because the car won't start”, the word “because” points back to the reason. We can call words like these indicator words.

Indicator words help, but they never settle the matter by themselves. Many arguments carry none at all, and a word like “since” can also mean “ever since”, which has nothing to do with reasons. When the clue is missing or doubtful, go back to asking what the speaker wants you to accept.
“If the battery is charged, the torch lights. The battery is charged. Therefore the torch lights.” Decide the role of the last sentence.

reveal.text: Check your choice against the sentences before it. The first two are premises, and the last is the conclusion they support.

lead.text: So far the conclusion has come last, but it does not have to. Compare two ways of saying the same thing: “The ferry is cancelled, so we'll drive” and “We'll drive, because the ferry is cancelled.” The conclusion, that we'll drive, moves from the end to the front. The premise moves with it from front to back, and the reasoning is the same in both.

That is why position can't be the test. A passage may begin with its conclusion, end with it or tuck it into the middle, and a speaker who has made a point may go on to defend it for several sentences. What stays fixed is the job each claim does. The conclusion is the claim being supported, and a premise is a claim doing the supporting, wherever it appears.
A longer passage shows this better. The next screen works through one, asking at each line what the speaker wants.

steps.headline: “We must leave now, because the last train is at nine and it is half past eight.” Which claim is the conclusion?

lead.text: Work through the passage a line at a time, starting from what the speaker wants.

workedSteps.text: Ask what the speaker wants you to accept.
Everything else is offered as a reason. The train time and the clock are premises, even though they come last.
workedSteps.math: Premises: the train is at nine; it is half past eight

workedSteps.text: The conclusion is the claim the premises support.

lead.text: Now a passage that begins with the claim it wants you to accept, and gives its reasons afterwards.

The torch argument can be written in the letters of the last lesson. Let p be “The battery is charged” and q be “The torch lights”. The first premise becomes p → q and the second is p. The conclusion is q. Written as “p → q; p; therefore q”, the argument loses the torch and keeps its shape.

Letters give us something to check against. Each row of a truth table is one way things could be, and a premise only does its job in a row where it holds. So to see what a set of premises amounts to, look for the rows where all of them hold at once. Take two plain premises, p and q on their own. Each is true in two rows, and both are true together only in the row TT.

afterFigure.text: Premises that must all hold narrow the rows down, and the conclusion is judged against whatever rows are left. The next question asks you to do that narrowing for the torch premises.

lead.text: Let p be “The battery is charged” and q be “The torch lights”. The premises are p → q and p. Look through the four rows, TT, TF, FT and FF.
A different argument, with its premises in another shape. Find the conclusion as before.

lesson.orientation: Separate an argument's conclusion from the claims offered in its support.
lesson.nextAction: Judge whether a conclusion follows separately from whether the premises are true.

blocks.text: The last lesson ended with a table of letters, and nobody talks like that. A friend on your doorstep says, “You should take an umbrella, because the forecast says rain.” A café sign says, “Go early, since the queue is shortest before nine.” Each remark tries to bring you round to something, and each hands you a reason for it.

In ordinary talk the aim and its reason arrive in one breath, and either can come first. Before you can ask whether the reasoning is any good, you have to know which part is which. If you mistake the reason for the aim, you spend your attention checking the wrong sentence.

This lesson takes a few remarks like these apart. It looks for what the speaker is after, then for the clues they leave behind, and it ends by putting one remark back into the letters of the last lesson so that the table can check it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll pick out the conclusion and the premises of a short argument, wherever they appear.

recap.keyIdea: The conclusion is the claim an argument wants you to accept. The premises are the claims offered in support, wherever they sit.

blocks.text: You asked what each speaker was after, and treated words like “so” and “because” as clues that need checking. You then saw that a conclusion can come first, and found that only one row of the table had both torch premises true.

recap.nextHook: Finding the conclusion is the first step. A conclusion may follow from its premises or may not, and that is a separate matter from whether the premises are true. The next lesson takes an argument about a dragon and pulls the two apart.

questions.prompt: In this argument, is “The torch lights” a premise or a conclusion?
hints: Which statement are the other sentences offered to support?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the conclusion supported by the two premises.

questions.onCorrect: Conclusion. The first two sentences are the support, and “therefore” introduces what they support.

misconceptions.feedback: A premise is offered as support. Is “The torch lights” offered to support something, or supported?

questions.prompt: How many rows make both p → q and p true?
hints: First keep the rows with p true.
Of those, drop any row where p → q is false.
Count the rows that satisfy both premises at once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only TT makes both premises true.

questions.onCorrect: One. Only TT makes both premises true, and q is true in that row.

misconceptions.feedback: Two rows have p true. Is p → q true in both?
Both premises have to hold in the same row. Test p first.
Go through the four rows and test both premises in each.

questions.prompt: “The torch lights, because the battery is charged and a charged battery makes it light.” In this passage, is “The battery is charged” a premise or a conclusion?
hints: A sentence's role depends on what it supports, not where it sits.
What is the charged battery offered as a reason for?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It supplies support, so it is a premise.

questions.onCorrect: Premise. It is offered as a reason for the torch lighting, though it comes later in the passage.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage starts with its conclusion. Is the battery being charged what the speaker wants you to accept, or a reason for it?

questions.prompt: “Either the parcel is at the desk or it is in the locker. It is not at the desk. Therefore it is in the locker.” Which location is the conclusion: desk or locker?
hints: The first two sentences support that one.
questions.onCorrect: Locker. “Therefore” introduces it, and the two earlier claims support it.

misconceptions.feedback: The desk appears in the premises. Which claim comes after “therefore”?

questions.prompt: What do we call a claim offered as support for a conclusion?
hints: This is the supporting part of an argument.
Tell the evidence apart from the claim it is meant to establish.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A premise is offered in support of the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: A premise. It supports the conclusion; it is not what the argument wants you to accept.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion is what the support is for. What is the support called?

questions.prompt: In “p → q; p; therefore q”, which letter is the conclusion?
hints: The two earlier statements support that letter.
questions.onCorrect: q. It follows “therefore”, and the two earlier statements are offered as its support.

misconceptions.feedback: p appears in the premises. Which letter follows “therefore”?

questions.prompt: Which claim is Sam trying to get you to accept: the umbrella or the forecast? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim is the reason, and which is the thing the reason is for?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sam wants you to take an umbrella. The forecast is the reason given.

questions.onCorrect: Taking an umbrella is what Sam wants. The forecast is offered as the reason.

misconceptions.feedback: Sam gives the forecast as a reason. What is it a reason for?

questions.prompt: “It will rain, so the match is off.” Which claim is the conclusion: the rain or the match? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim is offered as the reason for the other?
Ask what the speaker wants you to accept.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “So” points to the conclusion: the match is off.

questions.onCorrect: The match is off. The rain is the reason given, and it is meant to support the match being off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reason given. What does it support?

questions.prompt: Why isn't “the last train is at nine” the conclusion, even though it comes last?
hints: Ask what the speaker wants you to accept.

acceptedIdeas: Position doesn't decide; it supports the claim that we must leave.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position doesn't decide. The train time is offered as a reason to leave.

questions.onCorrect: Where a claim sits doesn't decide its role. It is a premise because it supports the claim that we must leave.

choices.label: Position doesn't decide; it supports the claim that we must leave.
The last sentence is never a conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: A conclusion can come last. Here it just doesn't.

questions.prompt: “Since the shop is shut on Sundays and today is Sunday, you can't buy bread today.” Which claim is the conclusion?
hints: Which claim do the other two support?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two “since” claims support that you can't buy bread today.

questions.onCorrect: You can't buy bread today. “Since” introduces the two premises that support it.

choices.label: The shop is shut on Sundays.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a reason offered after “since”. What does it help to support?
That follows “since”, so it is a reason. Which claim does it support?
